---
title: "Conformance, Assessment and Certification"
---

**Scope:** What you actually conform to, who can claim it, the three flavours of assessment, and what an auditor spends their time on.

**Status:** Working notes. Paraphrased for orientation only — `29110-4-1` and `29110-3` are authoritative.

---

## 1. You Conform to Part 4, Not Part 5

The most common mistake in the whole series is conflating the guide with the specification.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    G["<b>29110-5-1-2</b><br/>Management and<br/>engineering guide<br/><br/><i>should</i> · activities · tasks<br/>roles · work products"]
    S["<b>29110-4-1</b><br/>Profile specification<br/><br/><i>shall</i> · process requirements<br/>+ mapping to 12207"]
    G -->|"you read and follow this"| W["Your project"]
    W -->|"is audited against this"| S
    S -.->|"the guide is one way<br/>to satisfy the spec"| G
```

| | `29110-5-1-2` (guide) | `29110-4-1` (specification) |
|---|---|---|
| Modal verb | *should* | **shall** |
| Content | 10 activities, ~60 tasks, 23 work products, roles, tools | Process purposes and requirement statements |
| Function | Tells you how to work | States what must be true |
| Role in an audit | Evidence of a reasonable method | **The conformance target** |

The specification's requirements are terse by comparison — the PM process requirements are roughly a dozen `shall` statements covering scope definition, task and resource definition, feasibility, estimation, resource allocation, an execution plan agreed by the customer, risk identification and monitoring, a software version control strategy including backup and restoring, configuration item identification and control, progress monitoring and reporting, and corrective action on deviations.

That is the whole PM bar. The guide's four activities and dozens of tasks are one well-worked route to clearing it — not the only conceivable one, but the one that comes with free supporting material and no argument.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why the outcomes are worded oddly

Process outcomes in the specification are deliberately **not** written in the present tense. The reason is portability: the same outcome statements have to serve auditing for conformity, process-capability assessment, and organisational-maturity assessment. Wording them tenselessly keeps them neutral across all three.
:::

---

## 2. Who May Claim What

Three rules, and the third catches people out.

**A VSE claiming conformance must identify the profile.** Not "we are 29110 conformant" — *"we conform to the Software Engineering Basic Profile"*. The claim names the profile group and the profile, or it says nothing. See [Profile Groups and Profiles](profile-groups.qmd).

**Conformance can be claimed to the process part of the profile** when the VSE meets *all* mandatory process requirements of the specification, plus the associated properties and requirements in the base standards where applicable.

**Tool and course vendors cannot claim conformance at all.** The specification contains no requirements applicable to products that merely *facilitate* implementation — methods, courses, teaching aids, tools, forms. There is no such thing as a "29110-conformant issue tracker."

::: {.callout-warning}
## What that means when you are buying

A vendor advertising a "29110-compliant" template pack, ALM tool or training course is making a claim the standard explicitly does not support. The honest version of that claim is *"supports implementation of"*. Treat the difference as a signal about how carefully the vendor has read the thing they are selling.
:::

Two further facts about the claim itself:

- It **can be attested by a third party** — that is the certification route.
- It **can be mandated as part of procurement and contractual processes** — which is the commercial reason 29110 exists at all. A customer can require it in a tender.

---

## 3. Three Levels of Assessment

Part 3 defines certification schemes, assessment guidelines and compliance requirements covering three distinct things. They are frequently confused because all three are called "assessment".

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    A["<b>Self-assessment</b><br/><br/>Who: you<br/>Why: process improvement,<br/>gap analysis before anything else<br/>Output: a to-do list<br/>Tooling: the self-assessment DP"]
    B["<b>Conformity assessment</b><br/><br/>Who: an auditor<br/>Why: demonstrate the shall-statements<br/>of 29110-4-1 are met<br/>Output: pass / findings"]
    C["<b>Process capability assessment</b><br/><br/>Who: a qualified assessor<br/>Why: rate how well processes<br/>are performed<br/>Output: capability profile"]
    A -->|"cheap, repeatable,<br/>start here"| B
    B -->|"optional, separate<br/>question"| C
```

| | Self-assessment | Conformity assessment | Capability assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Question | Where are our gaps? | Do we meet the requirements? | How well do we perform? |
| Answers to | Yourselves | Customer, certification body | Improvement programme |
| Binary? | No | Essentially yes | No — it is a rating |
| Needed for certification? | No | **Yes** | No |

**Certification** is the third-party attestation built on a conformity assessment. Part 3 is addressed to the people running that process — auditors, certification bodies, accreditation bodies, and the sponsor of the audit — which is exactly why a VSE only needs to read it shortly before being audited.

Start with the **self-assessment deployment package** (see [Deployment Packages](deployment-packages.qmd)). It is free, it produces a gap list, and running it twice — once at the start and once before booking an audit — is the cheapest risk reduction available.

## 4. Before Anything: The Minimal Conditions

The specification states conditions assumed to already hold before the Basic profile can be used at all:

| # | Condition |
|---|---|
| 1 | There is a **project contract or agreement with scope** |
| 2 | Cost, technical and schedule **feasibility was performed before the project start** |
| 3 | The project working team, **including the project manager, is assigned and trained** |
| 4 | Goods, services and infrastructure are available |

The guide adds a fifth: the **development cycle is documented**.

These are pre-conditions, not tasks — nothing in the process produces them. A project that began without a documented, baselined agreement cannot retro-fit condition 1 by writing one now and dating it. Fix this before the project starts or accept the finding.

---

## 5. What an Auditor Actually Checks

Everything in the profile reduces to one question asked repeatedly:

> **Did this work product reach the state the standard requires, and can you show the transition?**

Possession of a file proves nothing. The evidence is the transition — `initiated → verified/validated → approved → baselined`. The current guide defines these states precisely; the ones that carry weight:

| State | What it asserts |
|---|---|
| **Initiated** | The workflow for the work product has begun |
| **Preliminary** | Exists but has not yet been submitted for approval |
| **Reviewed** | Presented to the authorised customer or stakeholder for comment |
| **Evaluated** | Has been verified **and** validated |
| **Approved** | An authorised stakeholder checked it is ready for delivery and signed off |
| **Baselined** | Approved **and** uploaded to the repository — a stable base for further development |
| **Corrected** | Identified defects have been removed |
| **Recovered** | Successfully restored from a repository — the word that makes backup verification mandatory |
| **Delivered** | Approved by the customer or authorised stakeholder and handed over |

::: {.callout-important}
## Approved ≠ baselined

`Approved` is a *judgement* by a person with authority. `Baselined` is approved **plus** stored in the controlled repository. Two separate events, and an audit can fail on the gap between them: a design document that everyone agreed to in a meeting but that never landed in version control is approved and not baselined.

The Git-native reading: approval is the review sign-off; baselining is the merge plus tag. Both need to be visible.
:::

### The five findings to expect

Ordered by how often they land, drawing on the [work product cheatsheet](iso29110-work-product-cheatsheet.qmd):

1. **Traceability record (WP.21)** — no native tooling produces it, so it is either automated or absent. There is no partial credit.
2. **Repository backup recovery (WP.12)** — the `recovered` state means a *restore* was demonstrated. A backup that has never been restored is not evidence.
3. **Verification and validation records (WP.22, WP.23)** — PM.O7 has no dedicated activity, so quality assurance is only ever evidenced by this accumulated pile. Teams that verify informally have nothing to show.
4. **Progress status record (WP.09)** — must cover cost and effort actuals and **the reason for each deviation**, not just task completion. Issue trackers do not carry money.
5. **Correction register vs change request (WP.04 vs WP.03)** — plan deviations and product changes are different registers with different lifecycles. Conflating them is the most common conceptual error in the profile.

## 6. A Realistic Path

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    A["<b>0. Scope the VSE</b><br/>which department or project<br/>is claiming conformance"]
    B["<b>1. Satisfy the minimal conditions</b><br/>agreement · feasibility · trained team ·<br/>infrastructure · documented lifecycle"]
    C["<b>2. Self-assess</b><br/>self-assessment DP → gap list"]
    D["<b>3. Close gaps in risk order</b><br/>version control strategy → project plan →<br/>requirement IDs → V&V records → traceability"]
    E["<b>4. Run one real project end to end</b><br/>PM.01→PM.04 and SI.01→SI.06,<br/>producing the work products as you go"]
    F["<b>5. Self-assess again</b><br/>this time against real evidence"]
    G["<b>6. Conformity assessment</b><br/>third-party audit, if the<br/>commercial case justifies it"]
    A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F --> G
```

Step 5 is the one people cut, and it is the cheapest step in the diagram.

Whether step 6 is worth it is a commercial question, not an engineering one. Certification buys admissibility in tenders that ask for it. If nobody is asking, steps 0–5 deliver essentially all of the engineering benefit — a disciplined plan, controlled versions, traceable requirements, and evidence you verified your own work.

---

## 7. Compressed

```
CONFORM TO      29110-4-1  (shall)      — the specification
FOLLOW          29110-5-1-2 (should)    — the guide
READ FOR AUDIT  29110-3                 — schemes and assessment

The claim must name the profile:
   "conformant to the Software Engineering Basic Profile"
Tool and course vendors cannot claim conformance at all.

Three assessments, often confused:
   self  → gaps        conformity → shall-statements
                       capability → how well

The audit question, asked 23 times:
   did this work product reach its required STATE,
   and can you show the transition?

approved  = a person with authority signed off
baselined = approved AND in the controlled repository
```
